title: Ten years of the 9/21 EMA crossover on NQ: half the profit went to fees
author: person-person12
selftext:
The 9/21 EMA cross is the first strategy almost everyone gets handed. The 9 crosses above the 21 and you go long, crosses below and you go short. Its in every beginner video and its in half the paid courses too, so I ran it in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) on NQ 15 minute candles from mid 2016 to the end of 2025 and let it trade both directions.

Rules were 1.5 ATR stop, 3 ATR target, regular hours only, flat before the close, one contract on a 100k account. No filter, no trend check, no news rule, the way its actually taught.

**NQ 15m, May 2016 to Dec 2025, 100k account, 1 contract:**

* 3,808 trades
* 40.9% win rate
* profit factor 1.02
* net **+33.86%**, 100k finished at about 133.8k
* max drawdown **35.55%**

Nearly a decade, almost four thousand trades, and it ends up 34% ahead while NQ itself roughly tripled.

**\_\_\_\_**

Heres the part I think matters more than the return. **Those exact same trades made +71.94% before execution costs.** Commission and slippage took **$38,080** out of it, so more than half the gross profit went to the cost of trading rather than to me. And the assumptions were not harsh: half a tick of slippage per side and $2.50 a contract, which is roughly what a retail futures account actually pays.

Thats the thing a cross over a cross cant survive. **Its a strategy with no entry filter, so it trades constantly**, and at 3,808 trades the bill is an input to the result rather than a rounding error on it. One extra tick of slippage per side is another $19k and this whole thing is flat.

Its a bit like a delivery job that pays $70 a day where the fuel comes to $38. The job isnt a scam and the number on the invoice is real, you just end up taking home a fraction of what the headline said, and youd have made more leaving the van parked.

**\_\_\_\_**

Two things id want somebody to say to me if this was my strategy getting pulled apart.

A 1.02 profit factor over 3,808 trades isnt a broken idea, its an idea sitting right on the line. The crossover does identify trend, it just has no opinion about whether the trend is worth paying to enter. Add almost any filter that cuts the trade count (a higher timeframe direction check, a minimum ATR, skipping the chop between 11am and 2pm) and the cost line falls with it. Thats also the honest version of why so many courses bolt five confluences onto a moving average cross: the extra conditions arent magic, they just stop you paying the toll four hundred times a year.

Two choices in here that change what got measured and that someone will reasonably object to. The 1.5 ATR stop and 3 ATR target are mine, not the strategys, because the crossover as taught has no stop at all. And flattening before the close caps what the winners could have become on the days the trend ran overnight.

I'll run it with a daily trend filter on the same window next and post that whichever way it falls.

comments.author: Square-Middle-4474
comments.body:
I trade this setup every day. What's interesting is the attitude that you can find a "Set it and forget it" solution via backtest and then let it run. I show my students how to evaluate price action for the context in which this setup works. Once you understand why context is critical, it turns everything around. Get yourself together. or not.

Good luck

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Youre right that the context decides it and a cross on its own is nothing, i dont disagree with that part. What id push back on is that **context can almost always be written down**, and if it cant then theres no way to tell whether the setup or the read is doing the work. How do you define the context you teach?

replies.author: Square-Middle-4474
replies.body:
As with most important concepts, not something I can provide in this setting. Takes too long. Professionals are usually trained by their employer or obtain third party training from professionals like myself. What I will say is that context has hierarchy, All professionals learn how to identify "Key References", and from that basic knowledge they proceed to document how price behaves each time a Key Reference is tested. This is how a professional proceeds to go from random to predictable behavior. The rest is about learning Industry Accepted Best Practice. If you read the other posts, you may notice that no one talks about it this way. Its the "blind leading the blind" on this website. That is why I suggest people start by improving their education. Very few are willing to do it, and that is why most (amateurs) never get very far.

For readers who actually want to move ahead, you can start with books by Larry Harris ("Trading and Exchanges: Market Microstructure for Practitioners") or Anna Coulling ("A Complete Guide to Volume Price Analysis"). Required reading at Top Tier Universities.

Good Luck

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
The bit i'd push on is "document how price behaves each time a Key Reference is tested". Thats a real process. The problem is that which reference counts, and what counts as a test, are both **your call on the day**, so two people running it properly end up with different records and neither one can check the other.

I ran the EMA cross because it was the version anybody could mark the same way twice. Whats your definition of a Key Reference that two traders would draw identically?
